entries.lesson_core_move: Express a periodic continuous-time signal in complex-exponential Fourier series form as a sum of integer-harmonic terms C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t} with each coefficient weighting one harmonic.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Complex-Exponential Fourier Series Form
sections.learning_goal: Recognize the standard complex-exponential Fourier series template and explain how $C_k$, $k$, and $\omega_0$ assign one coefficient to each harmonic.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the lesson is entirely notation-based.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the compact form $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$ and the role of the integer index in naming each harmonic.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start from a periodic signal with a DC term and a single positive/negative harmonic pair, then generalize to all integer harmonics.
paragraph_plan: State that a periodic signal can be written as a sum of complex exponentials at integer multiples of the fundamental angular frequency.
Introduce the symbols $C_k$, $k$, and $\omega_0$, and explain that each coefficient weights one harmonic term.
Show the full series template and emphasize that $k$ runs over all integers, including $k=0$.
Separate the DC term from the positive and negative harmonic terms so the indexing pattern is easy to read.
Close by naming the form as the reusable pattern students will use throughout the module.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the explanation narrow: define the template, the index, and the harmonic meaning, but do not derive coefficients or convert from trigonometric form.

sections.section_title: Writing a Periodic Signal as a Complex Harmonic Sum
sections.learning_goal: Write the compact complex-exponential series that matches an explicit list of DC, positive-harmonic, and negative-harmonic terms.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the task is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; choose the correct compact series expression.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the compact series form that matches a finite list of DC, positive, and negative harmonic terms.
distractor_plan: Include one option that omits the $C_0$ term.
Include one option that uses the wrong sign on one or more exponents.
Include one option that shifts the harmonic index by one.
Include one option that leaves the terms as a partial explicit sum instead of collapsing them into the $\sigma$ notation.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given the explicit harmonic terms $C_{-2} e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$, $C_{-1} e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, $C_0$, $C_1 e^{j\omega_0 t}$, and $C_2 e^{j2\omega_0 t}$, write the signal in compact complex-exponential Fourier series form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Collapse the explicit DC, positive-harmonic, and negative-harmonic terms into the standard integer-index sum $\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first example after the definition, so the only new move is collapsing named harmonic terms into the compact $\sigma$ notation.
solution_step_plan: Identify the DC term as the $k=0$ contribution.
Group the positive and negative harmonic terms by integer index.
Rewrite the explicit list as a single sum over all integers.
Confirm that each coefficient still weights exactly one harmonic.
practice_variation_axes: Change the largest harmonic index in the explicit list.
Change whether the finite list is written from low to high index or high to low index.
Change the coefficient labels while keeping the harmonic structure the same.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example symbolic and compact; do not derive coefficients or convert from trigonometric form. Later questions should mirror the same structure with only a small index or sign change.

sections.section_title: Substituting the Fundamental Frequency into the Series Form
sections.learning_goal: Replace $\omega_0$ with a stated value while preserving the harmonic indexing pattern of the series.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the task is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; choose the correctly substituted series expression.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the same series after substituting a stated period or fundamental angular frequency.
distractor_plan: Include one option that leaves $\omega_0$ symbolic instead of substituting it.
Include one option that uses the wrong numerical frequency factor.
Include one option that changes the sign of the exponent.
Include one option that confuses $T_0$ with $\omega_0$ inside the exponential.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For a periodic signal with period $T_0=4$, substitute $\omega_0=\pi/2$ into $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Carry out the substitution cleanly so the exponent becomes $jk(\pi/2)t$ and every coefficient term keeps the same index.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The structure stays the same; the only new wrinkle is a concrete numerical fundamental frequency.
solution_step_plan: State the given fundamental angular frequency from the period.
Substitute that value everywhere $\omega_0$ appears.
Leave the coefficient pattern and integer index range unchanged.
Check that the exponent still has the form $jk\omega_0 t$ after substitution.
practice_variation_axes: Change the period and therefore the numerical value of $\omega_0$.
Change whether the substitution is written in terms of $T_0$ or directly in terms of $\omega_0$.
Change the harmonic index shown in the worked line while keeping the substitution logic the same.

sections.handoff_notes: Center the example on substituting a concrete $\omega_0$; later questions should vary only the stated period or frequency value.

sections.section_title: Expanding the Sum into Indexed Harmonic Terms
sections.learning_goal: Expand a finite $\sigma$ expression into explicit harmonic terms and keep the integer index pattern intact.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the task is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; choose the correct expanded finite sum.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the explicit expansion of a small finite sum over integer harmonic indices.
distractor_plan: Include one option that leaves the $\sigma$ notation unexpanded.
Include one option that drops the negative-index terms.
Include one option that omits the $k=0$ DC term.
Include one option that writes the terms in the wrong index order.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Expand $\sum_{k=-2}^{2} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$ into explicit harmonic terms.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: List every term from $k=-2$ through $k=2$ so the student sees the DC term and the matching positive and negative harmonics.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Instead of keeping the compact $\sigma$ notation, the example expands the finite sum into named terms.
solution_step_plan: Read the lower and upper index bounds from the $\sigma$ notation.
Write the negative-index terms in a consistent order.
Include the $k=0$ DC term explicitly.
Verify that each term has the correct exponent $jk\omega_0 t$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the index bounds.
Change whether the expansion is ordered from negative to positive indices or vice versa.
Change one coefficient label while preserving the harmonic exponents.

sections.handoff_notes: Use the finite expansion to reinforce index reading and explicit term order; later questions should vary the bounds, not the underlying form.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Coefficient Weight on a Harmonic Term
sections.learning_goal: Match a displayed harmonic term to the coefficient that weights it in the complex-exponential Fourier series.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the task is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; choose the correct coefficient label.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask which coefficient weights a given positive or negative harmonic term, or which harmonic term corresponds to a given coefficient label.
distractor_plan: Include one option with the neighboring index.
Include one option with the opposite-sign index.
Include one option that names the exponential term instead of the coefficient.
Include one option that confuses the coefficient label with the harmonic frequency.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given the term $C_{-3} e^{-j3\omega_0 t}$, identify the coefficient that weights that harmonic.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Match the exponent index to the coefficient subscript and keep the sign straight.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The structure is now a single displayed harmonic term instead of a whole series; the task is to read the coefficient directly from the subscript.
solution_step_plan: Read the harmonic index from the exponential term.
Match that index to the coefficient subscript.
Keep the sign of the index consistent between the term and the coefficient.
Confirm that only the coefficient is being named, not the exponential term itself.
practice_variation_axes: Change the harmonic index sign.
Change the harmonic index magnitude.
Ask for the coefficient from the term or the term from the coefficient.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the emphasis on matching a displayed term to its coefficient; later questions should isolate a single term and test index and sign recognition.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret each complex Fourier coefficient C_k as the magnitude-and-phase weight assigned to the kth complex-exponential harmonic in a periodic signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Complex Fourier Coefficients
sections.learning_goal: Read $C_k$ as the complex weight on the $k$th complex-exponential harmonic in $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$, with magnitude giving the harmonic strength and phase giving its offset.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; keep the introduction entirely symbolic and text-based.

question_policy.answer_format: Not applicable for a tutorial section.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Not used in the tutorial step.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the learner to interpret each $C_k$ as the complex weight on the $k$th harmonic in $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$, then split that weight into magnitude and phase.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a signal with one visible harmonic term, such as $x(t)=C_0+C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}$, so the learner can read $C_1$ as the 1st-harmonic weight before generalizing to any $k$.
paragraph_plan: Start from the complex Fourier series form and point to the coefficient attached to each exponential term.
Explain that the subscript $k$ names the harmonic and that $C_k$ is a complex weight, not just a scalar label.
Show the polar reading $C_k=|C_k|e^{j\angle C_k}$ so magnitude and phase have separate jobs.
Close by stating that a list of coefficients is a compact description of which harmonics are present and how strongly each one appears.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not used in the tutorial step; later example sections handle the worked examples.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: N/A for the tutorial step.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: N/A for the tutorial step.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section compact and symbolic. Establish the interpretation of $C_k$ once, then let the example sections practice identifying the harmonic index, magnitude, phase, and nonzero harmonic set.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Harmonic Indexed by a Coefficient
sections.learning_goal: Identify which harmonic a coefficient $C_k$ weights by reading the subscript $k$ directly from the term $C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the task is to match coefficient subscripts to harmonic indices from notation alone.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with symbolic or short-text answers.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$, which harmonic does $C_{-2}$ weight?
distractor_plan: Use the wrong sign of the harmonic index.
Confuse the harmonic index with the angular frequency $\omega_0$.
Treat the term as the DC component.
Shift the harmonic number by one.
Replace the harmonic label with the coefficient value instead of the subscript.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: No separate direct-instruction block; this section is example-driven.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: In the term $C_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}$, identify which harmonic $C_3$ weights and explain why the subscript, not the exponential alone, tells you the harmonic number.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: State that $C_3$ weights the 3rd harmonic and that the index $3$ names the harmonic attached to $e^{j3\omega_0 t}$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first concrete read of the coefficient index after the tutorial's general definition.
solution_step_plan: Point to the coefficient $C_3$ and the matching exponential $e^{j3\omega_0 t}$.
Read the subscript as the harmonic index $k=3$.
State the harmonic in words as the 3rd harmonic.
Note that the coefficient's value is not needed yet, only its index.
practice_variation_axes: Positive versus negative harmonic index.
Harmonic name versus raw index notation.
Coefficient attached to a DC term versus an oscillatory term.
Index reading with a different harmonic order such as $k=4$ or $k=-2$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example narrow: one coefficient, one harmonic index, one clear readout. The later questions should mirror the same index-matching move while varying the sign or size of $k$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Coefficient Magnitude as Harmonic Weight
sections.learning_goal: Read $|C_k|$ as the strength or weight of the $k$th harmonic, separate from the phase carried by $C_k$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the magnitude reading should stay in symbolic polar form.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with a numeric or symbolic magnitude as the answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $C_4=6e^{-j\pi/5}$, what is the weight of the 4th harmonic?
distractor_plan: Use the phase angle instead of the magnitude.
Use the harmonic index instead of the coefficient weight.
Use the reciprocal of the magnitude.
Use the full complex coefficient instead of just the magnitude.
Use a negative or sign-flipped magnitude.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: No separate direct-instruction block; this section is example-driven.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $C_2=4e^{j\pi/6}$, state the weight of the 2nd harmonic and separate the magnitude from the phase.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Identify $|C_2|=4$ and state that the 2nd harmonic has strength 4, regardless of the phase.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This keeps the same coefficient-reading task but adds the magnitude-phase split of a complex coefficient.
solution_step_plan: Read the coefficient in polar form.
Identify the magnitude $|C_2|=4$.
State that the magnitude is the harmonic's weight or strength.
Leave the phase out of the weight claim.
practice_variation_axes: Different magnitudes and phases.
Ask for $|C_k|$ directly or for a comparison between two coefficients.
Include zero or fractional magnitudes.
Mix positive and negative indices while keeping the weight readout unchanged.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the magnitude read explicit and keep the phase out of the answer. The practice should stay close to a polar-form coefficient and ask for the harmonic's strength.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Coefficient Phase as Harmonic Phase
sections.learning_goal: Read $\angle C_k$ as the phase carried by the $k$th harmonic and keep it separate from the magnitude.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the task is to isolate the phase angle from the polar form of the coefficient.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with a phase angle or short symbolic phrase as the answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $C_1=2e^{-j\pi/6}$, what phase does the 1st harmonic carry?
distractor_plan: Use the magnitude instead of the phase.
Flip the sign of the phase angle.
Use the harmonic index instead of the phase.
Use the full complex coefficient instead of its angle.
Use zero as a generic distractor when the phase is nonzero.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: No separate direct-instruction block; this section is example-driven.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $C_{-1}=3e^{-j\pi/4}$, identify the phase of the $-1$st harmonic and keep it separate from the magnitude.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Identify the phase as $-\pi/4$ and state that the magnitude $3$ does not change the phase.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This uses the same polar-form reading as the previous section but switches the focus from magnitude to argument.
solution_step_plan: Identify the angle in $C_{-1}=3e^{-j\pi/4}$.
State the phase as $-\pi/4$.
Separate the phase from the magnitude $3$.
Connect the phase to the harmonic's shift or rotation.
practice_variation_axes: Positive versus negative phase angles.
Positive versus negative harmonic indices.
Ask for phase from polar form or from a coefficient table.
Use a different coefficient magnitude so the learner must ignore it.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the phase read explicit and keep the magnitude out of the answer. The later practice should mirror the same polar-form read while varying the angle and the harmonic index.

sections.section_title: Reading Nonzero Coefficients as Present Harmonics
sections.learning_goal: Scan a set of coefficients and identify exactly which harmonic indices are present by keeping the nonzero coefficients and dropping the zeros.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the learner can read presence and absence directly from a symbolic list of coefficients.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with symbolic text describing the set of present harmonics.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which harmonics are present if $C_{-2}=0$, $C_{-1}\neq 0$, $C_0=0$, $C_1\neq 0$, and $C_2=0$?
distractor_plan: Include coefficients that are zero as if they were present.
Forget the DC term when it is nonzero.
Collapse positive and negative harmonics into one choice incorrectly.
Add a harmonic that is not listed in the coefficient set.
Describe the strength of a harmonic instead of its presence.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: No separate direct-instruction block; this section is example-driven.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $C_{-2}=0$, $C_{-1}=2e^{j\pi/4}$, $C_0=3$, $C_1=0$, and $C_2=1e^{-j\pi/3}$, list the harmonics that are present in the signal and say which are absent.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Identify every nonzero coefficient as a present harmonic and every zero coefficient as an absent harmonic.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This combines the index read, the magnitude read, and the phase read into one spectrum-reading task.
solution_step_plan: Check each coefficient's value.
Mark every nonzero coefficient as a present harmonic.
Treat zero coefficients as absent harmonics.
Report the set of present indices, including $k=0$ if $C_0\neq 0$.
practice_variation_axes: Different zero and nonzero patterns.
Include or exclude the DC term.
Mix positive and negative harmonic indices.
Ask for the present harmonics as a set or list rather than as a sentence.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the synthesis step for the lesson. Keep the reading of the coefficient table symbolic, and make the distinction between present and absent harmonics completely explicit.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate complex Fourier coefficients by integrating x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0 t} over any one period and normalizing by the period to isolate the kth harmonic.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Coefficient Integral Over One Period
sections.learning_goal: Show that $C_k$ comes from multiplying $x(t)$ by $e^{-jk\omega_0 t}$, integrating over any one-period interval, and normalizing by $T_0$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the tutorial is built entirely from notation and orthogonality.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this step.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Introduce the coefficient integral as the one-period recipe for isolating $C_k$ from a periodic signal.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A periodic signal with one target harmonic and an interval of length $T_0$ starting at an arbitrary $t_0$.
paragraph_plan: State the complex Fourier series and name the coefficient integral that extracts $C_k$.
Show the product $x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0 t}$ inside the one-period integral and connect it to harmonic cancellation.
Explain why any interval of length $T_0$ works, not just $[0, T_0]$.
End with the operational recipe: choose $k$, multiply by $e^{-jk\omega_0 t}$, integrate over one period, and divide by $T_0$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the step focused on the setup and orthogonality recipe; do not move into a worked example or practice.

sections.section_title: Identifying T_0, omega_0, and k in the Coefficient Formula
sections.learning_goal: Read a coefficient formula and identify $T_0$, $\omega_0$, and $k$ before any integration.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is to read the coefficient notation correctly.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this step.

question_policy.answer_format: formula
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which coefficient formula correctly sets up $C_3$ for a signal with $T_0=2$ over the interval $[-1,1]$?
distractor_plan: Keep the right $T_0$ but use the wrong sign in the exponential.
Use the right exponential sign but the wrong harmonic index.
Use the right index but the wrong period in the denominator.
Forget the $1/T_0$ normalization.
Shift the interval correctly but write the exponent with $+jk\omega_0 t$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal has $T_0=2$. Identify the coefficient formula for $C_3$ over the one-period interval $[-1,1]$ and state the corresponding $\omega_0$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Read $T_0$ from the interval length, compute $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T_0}$, and substitute $k=3$ into the coefficient integral without evaluating it.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This step keeps the signal abstract but fixes a concrete period and interval so the learner practices translating notation into the coefficient setup.
solution_step_plan: Identify $T_0=2$ from the interval length.
Compute $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T_0}=\pi$.
Substitute $k=3$ into $e^{-jk\omega_0 t}$.
Write the normalized integral over $[-1,1]$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the period $T_0$.
Shift the start of the one-period interval.
Change the target harmonic $k$.
Hide $\omega_0$ and require computing it from $T_0$.

sections.handoff_notes: This is a setup-only example: force the reader to translate the notation into the correct coefficient formula before any integration starts.

sections.section_title: Computing C_k from a Smooth Periodic Formula
sections.learning_goal: Use the coefficient integral to extract the matching harmonic from a smooth trigonometric formula.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the coefficient is extracted from a symbolic trigonometric formula.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this step.

question_policy.answer_format: expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is $C_2$ for $x(t)=2+3\cos(\pi t)-4\sin(2\pi t)$ over one period?
distractor_plan: Use the coefficient from the cosine harmonic instead of the sine harmonic.
Flip the sign of the imaginary coefficient.
Return the DC term $2$.
Return $0$ by cancelling every term.
Add coefficients from different harmonics instead of isolating one term.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute $C_2$ for $x(t)=2+3\cos(\pi t)-4\sin(2\pi t)$ over one period.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Expand the trigonometric terms into complex exponentials and use orthogonality to isolate the matching $e^{j2\pi t}$ term.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first actual coefficient computation: the signal is smooth and periodic, but the writer must now carry out the integral rather than just identify the setup.
solution_step_plan: Write $C_2=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^2 x(t)e^{-j2\pi t}\,dt$.
Expand the cosine and sine terms into complex exponentials.
Use orthogonality to eliminate every term except the matching $e^{j2\pi t}$ term.
Read off the surviving coefficient and simplify to $2j$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the requested harmonic index.
Swap the sine and cosine amplitudes.
Change the signs on the harmonic terms.
Use a different smooth periodic formula with the same period.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the signal smooth and closed-form; the point is to practice coefficient extraction from a trigonometric sum.

sections.section_title: Computing C_k Over a Shifted One-Period Interval
sections.learning_goal: Show that shifting the one-period integration interval does not change the coefficient.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is to reuse the same coefficient setup on a shifted interval.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this step.

question_policy.answer_format: expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is $C_2$ for the same signal when the integral is taken over $[1,3]$ instead of $[0,2]$?
distractor_plan: Treat the shift as if it changes the coefficient.
Use the right interval length but the wrong harmonic index.
Forget the normalization by $T_0$.
Return the DC coefficient from the previous example.
Flip the sign of the correct complex coefficient.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use a shifted one-period interval and show, by periodicity or a change of variables, that the coefficient stays the same.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The signal and harmonic are unchanged; only the start of the integration interval moves by one period.
solution_step_plan: Write the coefficient integral over $[1,3]$.
Shift the variable or invoke periodicity to map the interval back to $[0,2]$.
Show the integrand matches the previous example after the shift.
Conclude that $C_2=2j$ again.
practice_variation_axes: Shift the interval by a different amount.
Keep the same period but choose another harmonic.
Use the same signal with a different one-period window.
Ask for the coefficient on a term that is not the one from the previous example.

sections.section_title: Splitting the Coefficient Integral Across Pieces of One Period
sections.learning_goal: Split a coefficient integral at each piece boundary and combine the partial results.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is to split a piecewise coefficient integral symbolically.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this step.

question_policy.answer_format: expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is $C_1$ for the two-piece periodic signal $x(t)=1$ on $0\le t<1$ and $x(t)=2$ on $1\le t<2$?
distractor_plan: Integrate only the first piece.
Integrate only the second piece.
Forget the $1/2$ normalization.
Use the wrong sign when evaluating the exponentials.
Treat the signal as if it were constant over the whole period.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute $C_1$ for the piecewise periodic signal $x(t)=1$ on $0\le t<1$ and $x(t)=2$ on $1\le t<2$, with $T_0=2$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to split the integral at the piece boundary, evaluate each piece, and combine the results into one coefficient.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The interval is still one period, but the signal now changes formula inside that interval, so the writer must split the integral before simplifying.
solution_step_plan: Write $C_1=\frac{1}{2}\left(\int_0^1 1\cdot e^{-j\pi t}\,dt+\int_1^2 2\cdot e^{-j\pi t}\,dt\right)$.
Integrate each piece separately.
Use $e^{-j\pi}=-1$ and $e^{-j2\pi}=1$ to simplify the endpoints.
Combine the two pieces and normalize to get $-\frac{1}{j\pi}$.
practice_variation_axes: Move the break point to another location inside the period.
Change one piece value or slope.
Ask for a different harmonic index.
Use three pieces instead of two.

sections.handoff_notes: The split at the signal boundary is the whole point; keep the algebra small and the interval exactly one period long.

sections.section_title: Checking That the Integral Isolates the kth Harmonic
sections.learning_goal: Verify by direct integration that only the matching harmonic survives over one period.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the goal is to verify harmonic isolation symbolically.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this step.

question_policy.answer_format: number
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is $C_2$ for $x(t)=1+2e^{j2\pi t}+7e^{j5\pi t}$ with $T_0=2$?
distractor_plan: Use the DC term as the answer.
Use the coefficient from the $k=5$ term.
Add the nonmatching coefficients together.
Return $0$ because only one term survives.
Double the matching coefficient before normalizing.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute $C_2$ for $x(t)=1+2e^{j2\pi t}+7e^{j5\pi t}$ with $T_0=2$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Multiply by the matching exponential, use orthogonality to kill every nonmatching term, and confirm that the integral returns only the $k=2$ coefficient.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This final example adds both a DC term and a second nonmatching harmonic so the writer must explicitly show that the integral isolates the requested harmonic.
solution_step_plan: Write the coefficient integral with $e^{-j2\pi t}$.
Distribute the product across the DC term, the $k=2$ term, and the $k=5$ term.

sections.section_title: Computing C_0 by Setting k=0 in the Coefficient Integral

sections.section_title: Interpreting C_0 as the Average Value Over One Period

Change the interval so the piecewise boundaries either align or misalign.
Vary the constant levels while keeping the same period length.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Interpret the pair $C_4e^{j4\omega_0 t}+C_{-4}e^{-j4\omega_0 t}$ as one nonzero harmonic component and state what harmonic number it represents.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Explain that the $\pm 4$ pair is one harmonic at frequency $4\omega_0$ and that the two coefficients together describe that single component.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from matching terms to interpreting the matched pair as one signal component.
solution_step_plan: Group the $+k$ and $-k$ terms together.
Name the harmonic number $k$.
State the frequency magnitude $k\omega_0$.
Explain that the coefficients jointly determine the component.
practice_variation_axes: Change the harmonic number.
Change whether the pair is written adjacent or separated.
Vary whether the prompt asks for a statement of meaning or a direct identification.
Include a neighboring pair as a distractor.

sections.handoff_notes: The key move is interpretation, not algebra: the pair should be read as one nonzero harmonic component.

sections.section_title: Separating Nonzero Harmonic Pairs from the DC Term
sections.learning_goal: Separate the unpaired DC term from all $\pm k$ harmonic pairs in a complete series.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; the grouping task is symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not request a diagram; keep the full-series grouping notation-based.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices labeled A-E; each choice is a term classification or grouping statement.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask which term is the DC component and which terms belong to each nonzero harmonic pair in a short complex Fourier series.
distractor_plan: Put $C_0$ into a harmonic pair.
Pair terms with different harmonic magnitudes.
Omit one side of a nonzero pair.
Mislabel a nonzero term as DC.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not used in example sections.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Separate the DC term from the nonzero harmonic pairs in $x(t)=C_0+C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}+C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}+C_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}+C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Identify $C_0$ as the unpaired zero-frequency term and group the remaining terms into the $\pm 1$ and $\pm 2$ harmonic pairs.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extend the pair interpretation to a full series by separating the DC term from all nonzero harmonic groups.
solution_step_plan: Isolate the $C_0$ term.
Group each positive term with its negative partner.
Name each nonzero harmonic number present.
State that the DC term is separate from every nonzero harmonic pair.
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of nonzero pairs.
Change which harmonic numbers appear.
Vary whether the DC term is first, last, or embedded in the middle.
Include a missing partner as a distractor.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the DC term separate from the nonzero harmonic pairs and make the grouping rule obvious.
